title: Run Your Love Life Like a CEO: 5 Frameworks For Dating
summary: The hosts translate business concepts into five dating frameworks for high-performing women who over-give: the CEO shift (choose, don't prove), emotional due diligence, patterns over potential, defining deal terms (non-negotiables), and emotional equity. They back it with McKinsey, Gottman and Pew data on invisible and emotional labor, offer a three-question litmus test, and close with a track-talk-request process for repairing imbalance rather than walking away.

ideas.idea: If a business partner missed deadlines and went dark for days you would end the deal, but high-performing women let it slide in dating and over-give to people who are not showing up.
ideas.detail: Framing for the episode: stop over-functioning and act like the CEO of your own life.

ideas.idea: Women are conditioned from childhood to be likeable and make others comfortable, and carry that invisible labor into both work and relationships.
ideas.detail: A 2021 McKinsey study shows women take on invisible labor like smoothing conflicts; the lone woman on a team gets 'voluntold' to plan happy hours, and as a Goldman analyst Jean was the only one of several analysts asked to compile the hundreds-page investment committee book every week, work you can only do right or screw up and that never helps promotion.

ideas.idea: Showing up fully for someone who has not chosen you is like waiting for a deal that is never going to close; a CEO makes the hire and the decisions rather than sitting on the sidelines.
ideas.detail: Examples: pouring in effort early on chemistry alone, or being the partner who is blamed if the wedding gift for his college friend does not show up. Mini exercise: name one way you shrink yourself in dating that you would never tolerate in business, then ask what your CEO self would do.

ideas.idea: Do emotional due diligence before getting serious, examining communication style, dating history and how they handle commitment, the way an investor checks financials and leadership before buying a company.
ideas.detail: Skipping the unsexy values conversations leaves you in the deep end wishing you had discussed the important topics before feeling so deeply.

ideas.idea: Both partners being committed to repair after conflict is one of the strongest predictors of a successful relationship; it is about whether you fight well and make up, not being perfect.
ideas.detail: Cited from the Gottman Institute; you can only learn this by seeing how someone communicates during a disagreement and how you move past it.

ideas.idea: Ask better questions on dates, like what happened in your last breakup and how you handle conflict, and notice how they talk about exes, friends and family.
ideas.detail: Cherie jokes 'I'm nosy, I want to know' to make the timing feel natural, whether on date one or date five.

ideas.idea: Words mean nothing without consistent action; in your 30s it is 'you say this, now show me'.
ideas.detail: Cherie says in her early 20s she was charmed by words of affirmation and promises that never had action behind them.

ideas.idea: Watch how someone handles discomfort, mistakes and things going wrong, and track whether you feel calm or on edge around them.
ideas.detail: Jean's tennis date: he proposed it, failed to book a court, got an attitude when someone claimed it, and she ended up doing unpaid emotional labor soothing him for his own mistake.

ideas.idea: High-achieving women drawn to projects fall into dating someone's potential instead of their patterns, and can wait months or years for the imagined version to appear.
ideas.detail: Cherie spent years on and off with someone she was more excited about as a future version; Jean says you can lose yourself putting your goals on the back burner for a partner who does not reciprocate, even without malice.

ideas.idea: Bring investor-style clarity and KPIs to relationships, expecting certain progress by certain milestones, because without intentionality romance slips into complacency.
ideas.detail: A strong connection without consistent follow-through is just a marketing campaign.

ideas.idea: Audit your own attraction and dynamic patterns, and break the ones that have not led to fulfillment.
ideas.detail: Cherie has two types, the stoic hot guy and the charismatic center-of-attention guy, and the second has not worked out; mini exercise: write down your last two or three relationship patterns and the early signs you ignored.

ideas.idea: Defining your deal terms (non-negotiables) is not high maintenance; it is setting filters that save your time and theirs, and you cannot expect someone to meet terms you have never articulated.
ideas.detail: Examples: only dating someone who takes accountability, or who plans a certain number of dates; write down two or three non-negotiables and recommit to one boundary you broke in the past.

ideas.idea: Being picked up from the airport is a legitimate non-negotiable if that is how you feel loved, and if someone cannot meet your terms that is not a failure but your filter working.
ideas.detail: Cherie was previously afraid to ask for this act of service though it meant a lot to her; she allows reasonable exceptions like work meetings, and notes LAX at 10 p.m. Sunday makes the effort mean even more.

ideas.idea: Emotional equity means both people put in effort to plan, solve problems and make things work, rather than one doing the heavy lifting while the other coasts.
ideas.detail: A 2023 Pew study found women in heterosexual relationships report carrying 2.5 times more emotional labor than men, and 65% feel overwhelmed.

ideas.idea: Three-question litmus test: after a date do you feel more or less like yourself; are you chasing their attention or asking whether they deserve yours; and if you stopped initiating would the connection die or deepen.
ideas.detail: You must pass all three, since fun dates that leave you feeling yourself can still come with no communication in between; the test applies to friendships too.

ideas.idea: Your attention, time, energy and love are your most valuable resources, so the opportunity cost of giving them to the wrong person, including rumination, is high.
ideas.detail: Time not spent on that person would go into growing yourself; someone living in your head rent-free is still consuming attention.

ideas.idea: Who you marry is the most important decision of your life: it affects finances, family, children and is the person you will share the most meals with, so run the litmus tests early.
ideas.detail: Marrying someone who causes more emotional strife than connection is a burden you can overcome but that creates a much bigger headache down the road.

ideas.idea: Noticing an imbalance does not mean ending the relationship; repair it in three steps: track the emotional labor for a week, talk about it with I-statements, and make a request rather than a demand.
ideas.detail: Example: 'I've noticed I've been buying all the wedding gifts for your friends, could we share that responsibility?' A real partner will co-create; a mismatch will resist or deflect, so either way you get your answer.

ideas.idea: The five frameworks are shift from proving to choosing, practice emotional due diligence, trust consistent behavior over potential, define your deal terms, and build emotional equity through shared effort.
ideas.detail: The episode is really about self-worth, power and confidence, entering relationships from clarity not scarcity; the power move is to make one decision using the frameworks this week.
